doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Harold Arlen scores and John Lewis's American Jazz Orchestra
summary: Saving the Arlen scores, the Cooper Union concert, and typical studio time.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: How about personal collections. Have you saved a lot of scores or recordings?

I saved the scores from the Harold Arlen album, because I’m proud of the writing I did for that. That led to something by the way. I got to know John Lewis at school because he was on the Board of Trustees. And when he organized, was a mentor of the American Jazz Orchestra and he did the concerts at Cooper Union, they did a concert based on Harold Arlen and Claude Thornhill, so who was a better natural? And he hired me to conduct, rehearse and conduct. They had — the orchestra was every big name in the city, you know Randy Brecker and on and on. And that was a pleasant thing too. I liked what I wrote for the Harold Arlen album, even though it’s not a jazz album. When John called
me I said that’s not a jazz album. He said, “We want the tunes.” He said, “We’re doing Harold Arlen.”
How long did you get in the studio to record the typical album?
Well the normal date was a three hour day. Usually you would do I think like this we did four days, I’m not sure. You know they give you a little extra day or something.
